concepts.name: The state and the government
concepts.description: The four features of a state, what a government is and why the words are confused.
concepts.idea: The state has people, land, government and sovereignty; the government is only one part and can change.
concepts.rule: A state (or nation) is a political organisation with authority to govern a defined territory and its population. It has four parts: people, land, government and sovereignty, the full power to make laws and decisions without outside control. Without a permanent population there is no state; tourists who visit do not form one. Boundaries are agreed with neighbouring states. The government is a group of people or system that runs the country: leaders, ministers and officials who make, enforce laws and resolve disputes. It can change after elections but the state remains, like teachers coming and going while the school stays. The words are mixed up because the government acts on behalf of the state and we mostly meet the government.
concepts.example: The state is like a school and the government is the principal and teachers.

concepts.name: The police, government departments and the people
concepts.description: The role of the police, how citizens relate to the government and the executive departments we meet in daily life.
concepts.idea: The police are part of state governments and protect people while respecting their rights.
concepts.rule: The police maintain law and order within each state and are part of the state government working with local communities. They are agents of the state who can legally use force to ensure safety free from crime and violence, work with courts and prisons, and promote safety through awareness programmes on road safety, drug abuse and women's safety, but must respect constitutional rights. People elect leaders to represent them, the police enforce laws and present cases to the judiciary, and the Constitution, laws and courts protect rights. Government departments, whose names we see on boards, implement policies made by the legislature; the judiciary ensures laws are followed. In daily life we mainly meet the executive.

concepts.name: Democracy, republic and protecting everyone's rights
concepts.description: The difference between democracy and republic, India as a democratic republic, protection of minorities and the tribal lands example.
concepts.idea: In a democratic republic the people elect the government and the head of state is elected within limits set by a constitution.
concepts.rule: Democracy means rule by the people (demos = people, kratos = rule): people choose their government through free and fair elections. A republic is a form of government where the head of state is elected, directly or indirectly, and not a hereditary monarch, and where the ruler's power is limited by a constitution or laws. A country can be both, like India or the USA. The UK, Canada and Sweden are democracies but not republics as they have monarchs. India's president is elected by a group of elected representatives. The Constitution guarantees fundamental rights so the majority cannot violate any citizen's rights, preventing 'dominance of the majority'. Mining was not allowed in the sacred hills of the Dongria Kondh. George Washington refused to become king in 1782.
concepts.example: The RWA changed its rule to exempt food and medicines, protecting a minority.

concepts.name: The legislature and the political and permanent executive
concepts.description: The legislature, the political executive, the permanent executive or bureaucracy and civil services.
concepts.idea: Elected leaders make big decisions while permanent civil servants run the government day to day.
concepts.rule: The legislature makes laws that apply to everyone; states have their own legislatures making laws for the state. The executive implements laws and takes policy decisions and has two parts. The political executive are elected leaders: the prime minister, chief ministers and ministers, and the president and governors, who mostly have formal roles. They serve a fixed time, usually five years. The permanent executive are officers selected through exams such as those by the UPSC, called bureaucrats or civil servants, who are not changed after elections and give expert advice, implement policies and manage services. Well-known services include IFS, IAS, IPS, IRS and IFoS. C.B. Muthamma became the first woman to join the Indian Foreign Service in 1949 and won a Supreme Court case against gender bias.

concepts.name: Government roles and how citizens can engage
concepts.description: Protector, provider and regulator roles, and ways citizens can act: grievance redressal, RTI, media, NGOs, letters and voting.
concepts.idea: Citizens can make government work for them through grievance offices, RTI, media, civil society, letters and voting.
concepts.rule: The government is protector (law and defence), provider (public welfare and infrastructure) and regulator (economic activity and social justice). Yet problems like corruption and poor services remain. Citizens can use grievance redressal offices and the Public Grievances Portal, ask for information under the Right to Information Act which brings transparency and accountability, use the media, engage through civil society organisations or NGOs, write to representatives and vote. In Bagepalli near Bengaluru an RTI on road spending helped citizens get poorly done roadwork fixed. In 1970 the Kerala Government planned a hydroelectric project in Silent Valley; NGOs, scientists and villagers opposed it, the Centre cancelled it in 1983 and it became a National Park in 1985.
concepts.example: The Silent Valley Movement saved rainforest from a dam.

concepts.name: The judiciary: guardian of the Constitution
concepts.description: What the judiciary does, judicial review, the rule of law and why independence matters.
concepts.idea: The independent judiciary protects rights, interprets laws and ensures everyone follows the law.
concepts.rule: The judiciary makes sure everyone follows the law. It settles disputes, protects people's rights and checks whether laws made by government are fair and just. It is independent, not controlled by government or politicians, so justice is fair and equal. Its functions are protecting and defending laws, interpreting laws when wording is complex or people disagree, protecting citizens' rights and liberty (we can go to court if fundamental rights are violated) and safeguarding the Constitution through judicial review, acting as a referee when government or others break the law. It protects the rule of law: everyone, even the government, must follow the law. Without a strong and fair judiciary, democracy cannot survive.
concepts.example: Judicial review lets courts check whether laws follow the Constitution.

concepts.name: Tiers of government and decentralisation
concepts.description: The three tiers, why India needs decentralisation, panchayats and municipalities, Gandhi's gram swaraj and the education example.
concepts.idea: Power is shared among union, state and local governments so that local problems are solved locally.
concepts.rule: India has three tiers of government: union (central), state and local. India has 28 states and 8 union territories and over 1.4 billion people, so a single government cannot meet all needs. The Constitution originally had only two levels; local governments were under the State List. In the early 1990s amendments created the panchayati raj system and municipalities as the third tier, strengthening democracy at the grassroots. Decentralisation means power is spread out and local problems are solved locally, with bigger issues by higher governments. Benefits are stronger local governments, better local knowledge, more democracy, local discussion and more accountability. The union looks after defence, foreign affairs and currency; states handle police, land, health and agriculture; local governments handle water, drainage and streetlamps. Gandhi advocated gram swaraj. In school education, Parliament and state legislatures make laws like the Right to Education Act, ministers and officers implement them and courts and bodies like NCPCR protect children's rights.
concepts.example: A broken streetlamp is fixed by the local municipal body, not the Central Government.
